analysis.one_liner: Requires ingredient labels, multilingual safety data sheets, and health research for salon cosmetics and products marketed to women of color.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it sat in two House committees from October 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require cosmetics made for professional salon use to list every ingredient on the package and on company websites. It would require safety data sheets for hazardous professional products, translated into Spanish, Vietnamese, Chinese, Korean, and other languages on request, and available to salon workers. It would also fund federal research into chemicals in products marketed to women and girls of color and used by nail, hair, and beauty salon workers, fund grants to design safer chemicals, and create an interagency council and advisory committee on cosmetic safety.
analysis.who_benefits: Professional nail, hair, and beauty salon workers — who are disproportionately low-wage women of color and immigrants — would learn what chemicals are in the products they handle all day, in languages they read, and get federally funded research and safer alternatives developed for their workplaces. Women and girls of color, who are marketed products with chemicals linked to health problems, would get targeted research, compliance review of those products, and a voice on a new FDA advisory committee. Minority-owned cosmetic companies would get grant priority to reformulate with safer ingredients.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Salon workers and women of color

how_it_helps.text: Requires every cosmetic intended for professional use to list each ingredient by prominence on the package and on the manufacturer's, distributor's, or seller's website, so salon workers and their clients can finally see what is in the products applied to them all day; unlabeled products would be treated as misbranded under federal law.

Requires OSHA to issue a standard making manufacturers and importers produce safety data sheets for hazardous professional cosmetics, post them online, and provide them in English, Spanish, Vietnamese, Chinese, Korean, and other languages on request — with salon owners required to keep the sheets in the workplace and give translated versions to exposed employees, which matters because many salon workers do not read English.

Authorizes $7.5 million for FDA research into the chemicals linked to adverse health effects that are most common in cosmetics marketed to women and girls of color, and another $7.5 million for research on chemicals used by professional nail, hair, and beauty salon workers, with results published so communities and workers can identify unsafe exposures.

Authorizes $10 million in grants to design cosmetic chemicals with no inherent toxicity, giving priority to replacing hazardous chemicals in salon products and products marketed to women and girls of color, and to helping minority-owned cosmetic companies create safer formulations.

Creates an Interagency Council on Cosmetic Safety spanning FDA, CDC, EPA, OSHA, and other agencies to share toxicity and exposure data, and requires FDA to set up a process — with a permanent advisory committee that includes representatives of women of color and salon workers — to review cosmetics marketed to women and girls of color for compliance with safety requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Cosmetics manufacturers, importers, and distributors would bear the cost of full ingredient labeling, posting ingredient lists on websites, and producing and translating safety data sheets. Taxpayers would fund the authorized research, grants, and council work — up to $25 million over five years. Small salons would carry a modest new duty to keep safety data sheets on hand and obtain translations for workers who ask.

drawbacks.text: The bill places new compliance costs on cosmetics manufacturers, importers, and distributors — full ingredient disclosure on labels and websites, plus safety data sheets translated into at least five languages — and gives salon employers a paperwork duty to keep sheets on site and provide translations, costs that fall heaviest on small firms.

It authorizes up to $25 million of federal spending over five years ($7.5 million for research on products marketed to women of color, $7.5 million for salon worker research, and $10 million for safer-chemical grants), an expense opponents would weigh against voluntary industry disclosure.

The bill does not ban or restrict any chemical outright; the research reports are not due until up to five years after the first grants are awarded, so even if enacted it would have delivered information and safer formulations slowly rather than immediate protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete for a specific, exposed population: workers who handle professional salon products daily and consumers, mostly women and girls of color, marketed products containing chemicals linked to health harm. The costs — labeling, translated data sheets, and $25 million in research spending over five years — are modest relative to the health stakes, and the grants would partly offset reformulation costs for small and minority-owned makers. The main honest criticism is pace: no chemical would be restricted, and full results would take years. On balance the bill is a low-cost disclosure-and-research measure whose failure left the affected workers and consumers with nothing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees, then to a health subcommittee, and no committee ever acted on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on October 8, 2021, joined by Rep. Lisa Blunt Rochester as the other original sponsor; 13 House Democrats cosponsored it and no Republican did.

The same day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and Labor Committee; three days later, on October 11, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
That subcommittee referral was the last action of any kind. The bill received no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cosmetics manufacturers came out ahead: without the bill they faced no federal requirement to disclose full ingredients for professional salon products or to provide translated safety data sheets, while the salon workers and women of color the bill was written to protect remain without those disclosures and without the funded research.

industries.industry: Cosmetics and personal care product manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have forced full ingredient disclosure on labels and websites for professional-use products and required safety data sheets in six or more languages — new compliance costs, and unwelcome visibility for chemicals currently hidden behind trade-secret fragrance and preservative labels. Its interest in avoiding disclosure ran directly against the safety interest of salon workers and consumers.

industries.industry: Professional hair, nail, and beauty salons and spas
industries.note: Salon owners would have taken on a modest duty to keep safety data sheets in the workplace and provide translations on request, but their predominantly low-wage, immigrant workforce would have gained the most from knowing what is in the products they handle; the bill is written around this industry's workers, not against its businesses.

The safer-chemicals grant program gives explicit priority to helping minority-owned companies that sell to women and girls of color or to salon workers reformulate with less hazardous ingredients, subsidizing a competitive advantage against larger incumbents.
